newsitem.title: JORDAN: Israel pumps Galilee water to Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Israel pumps Galilee water to Jordan.

text.p: King Hussein opened the floodgates on Tuesday to pump millions of cubic metres of water from Israel to Jordan's parched reservoirs, under a deal aimed at patching up a long-running dispute over water rights.
Officials said the king flicked a switch to pump 72,000 cubic metres of fresh water a day to Jordan's northern town of Adassiya from the Sea of Galilee, about 10 km (six miles) to the northwest.
The water supply accord, forged at a secret summit meeting this month, addresses Jordanian complaints that Israel has not honoured its water supply commitments under a 1994 peace treaty.
"This is an example of how you can reach agreement through dialogue," the king said. "It is one small step, but there is still a lot to achieve."
But even as the water flowed on Tuesday the two sides disputed the quantities.

Jordanian officials said the deal called on Israel to supply Jordan with 30 million cubic metres of drinking water a year, continuing until other water sources become available to Jordan, which faces major water shortages.
Israeli officials insisted the total supply would be just 25 million cubic metres a year, with a slightly higher flow in summer and decreased flow in winter, when Jordan's needs are less pressing.

The row broke out earlier this month when Jordan's Crown Prince Hassan refused to meet Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu in protest at what Jordan saw as persistent Israeli foot-dragging over meeting its commitments.
Israel pledged, in a vaguely worded clause in the 1994 peace treaty, to "cooperate in finding sources for the supply to Jordan" of 50 million cubic metres of drinking water a year.
Jordan, whose underground water aquifers are rapidly drying up, accused Israel of reneging on the deal. Israel says it is cooperating but is not obliged to supply the water itself.
Both sides say they want to build a desalination plant but need international funding to set up such a costly project.
Jordan says its citizens consume only about one quarter of the amount specified as "water poverty level".
